course.title: Chinese (Pinyin), Start to Fluent
course.subtitle: Mandarin Chinese from absolute beginner through everyday fluency — every lesson shown in pinyin only, so you can start speaking immediately without first learning to read Hanzi characters
course.heroLedeSuffix: Real sentences from lesson one, shown entirely in pinyin — audio is real native-quality Mandarin pronunciation, so your ear learns the real language while your eyes read Latin script.

a1-shi-tobe.title: The Verb 'To Be' (shì)
a1-shi-tobe.explanation: Chinese verbs never conjugate for person or number — shì ('to be') stays exactly the same whether the subject is I, you, he, or they. To negate, place bù directly before it: bú shì ('is not'). There is no equivalent of English am/is/are — just one unchanging word.
a1-shi-tobe.fact: shì is only used to link two nouns (X is Y). To describe a quality with an adjective (e.g. 'I am tall'), Chinese normally drops shì entirely and uses the adjective directly as the predicate: wǒ hěn gāo ('I am very tall') — no shì at all. Inserting shì there is one of the most common mistakes beginners make.

dialogue.en: Are you a student?

dialogue.native: Shì, wǒ shì xuéshēng. Nǐ ne?
dialogue.en: Yes, I am a student. And you?

dialogue.native: Wǒ bú shì xuéshēng, wǒ shì lǎoshī.
dialogue.en: I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.

a1-negation.title: Negation: bù vs méi
a1-negation.explanation: bù negates almost everything — verbs, adjectives, and future or habitual actions: wǒ bú qù ('I'm not going'), wǒ bù gāo ('I'm not tall'). méi, often as méiyǒu, negates possession ('don't have') and completed past actions: wǒ méiyǒu qián ('I don't have money'), wǒ méi chī zǎofàn ('I didn't eat breakfast'). Crucially, méi is never used with shì — 'is not' is always bú shì, never méi shì.
a1-negation.fact: bù changes tone before another fourth-tone syllable — it becomes second tone (bú) instead of fourth (bù), e.g. 'is not' is pronounced bú shì, not bù shì, even though the underlying word never changes, only the spoken tone. This is why you'll see both bù and bú written in these lessons.

dialogue.en: Do you have time?
Sorry, I don't have time.

dialogue.native: Méi guānxi, wǒmen míngtiān zài shuō.
dialogue.en: It's okay, we'll talk again tomorrow.

a1-questions.title: Yes/No Questions with ma
a1-questions.explanation: To turn any statement into a yes/no question, simply add the particle ma to the very end — no word order change, no auxiliary verb needed: nǐ shì xuéshēng ('You are a student') → nǐ shì xuéshēng ma? ('Are you a student?'). This is dramatically simpler than English question formation.
a1-questions.fact: ma can never be combined with a question word like shénme ('what') or shéi ('who') in the same sentence — a sentence already containing a question word is already a question, and adding ma on top is a common beginner error that native speakers immediately notice sounds wrong.

dialogue.native: Zhè shì nǐ de bēizi ma?
dialogue.en: Is this your cup?

dialogue.native: Bú shì, nà shì tā de.
dialogue.en: No, that's hers.
Then whose is this?

a1-measure-words.title: Measure Words (liàngcí)
a1-measure-words.explanation: Unlike English, Chinese requires a measure word between a number and almost every noun — you cannot say 'one book' as yī shū, you must say yì běn shū ('one [volume] book'). Different measure words go with different categories of noun: gè is the general, all-purpose measure word usable for most nouns when unsure; běn is for bound printed things like books; zhāng is for flat objects like paper or tickets; zhī is for many animals.
a1-measure-words.fact: gè alone can safely substitute for almost any specific measure word in casual speech and will still be understood — a genuinely useful shortcut for beginners, even though native speakers use the more precise word when they know it.

dialogue.en: How many dumplings would you like?

dialogue.native: Wǒ yào shí gè jiǎozi hé yì bēi chá.
dialogue.en: I'd like ten dumplings and a cup of tea.
Sure, coming right up.

a2-le-completed.title: Completed Actions (le)
a2-le-completed.explanation: The particle le placed right after a verb marks that the action is completed or has happened -- roughly like English's past tense, though le itself marks completion/change, not time. To negate a completed action, don't use bù + le together -- use hái méi (yǒu) + verb ('haven't ... yet') instead, and drop le entirely.
a2-le-completed.fact: le has two very different jobs that beginners often mix up: right after a verb (chī le, 'ate') it marks a completed action; at the very end of a sentence (Wǒ è le, 'I've become hungry') it marks a change of state. The same sentence can even carry both at once.

dialogue.en: Have you eaten?
Yes I have, thanks. And you?

dialogue.native: Wǒ hái méi chī. Wǒ è le.
dialogue.en: I haven't yet. I'm hungry.

a2-future.title: Future Actions (yào vs huì)
a2-future.explanation: Both yào and huì can point to the future, but they answer different questions. yào expresses intention or plan -- 'going to / want to' -- something you've decided to do. huì expresses either a learned ability ('can/know how to') or a prediction about what will happen, closer to English 'will'.
a2-future.fact: huì is also the word for skills you've learned, with no future meaning at all: Wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén ('I can speak Chinese') is about ability right now, not something that will happen later. Context, not the word itself, tells you which sense of huì is meant.

dialogue.en: What are you going to do this weekend?

dialogue.native: Wǒ yào qù kàn diànyǐng. Nǐ huì lái ma?
dialogue.en: I'm going to see a movie. Will you come?
Yes, I'll definitely come!

a2-comparison.title: Comparisons (bǐ)
a2-comparison.explanation: To say A is more [adjective] than B, put bǐ directly between the two things being compared, followed by a plain adjective -- no hěn or other degree word goes in front of it (that's for stating a quality alone, not comparing). To compare a specific amount, add the difference after the adjective: A bǐ B dà liǎng suì ('A is two years older than B').
a2-comparison.fact: For 'not as ... as', don't use bù bǐ -- that actually sounds like a debate over the comparison itself. The natural way is méiyǒu: A méiyǒu B (nàme) adjective, literally 'A doesn't have B's amount of that quality'.

dialogue.native: Zhège shǒujī bǐ nàge guì ma?
dialogue.en: Is this phone more expensive than that one?

dialogue.native: Bǐ nàge guì yìdiǎn, dànshì gèng hǎo yòng.
dialogue.en: It's a bit more expensive than that one, but easier to use.
Then I'll buy this one.

a2-because-so.title: Because...So (yīnwèi...suǒyǐ)
a2-because-so.explanation: Chinese pairs the two halves of a because-clause explicitly: yīnwèi introduces the reason, suǒyǐ introduces the result -- unlike English, where using both 'because' and 'so' in one sentence feels redundant, in Chinese it's the normal, expected pattern. Either half can also stand alone once the connection is already clear from context.
a2-because-so.fact: The reason-clause doesn't have to come first. Wǒ méi qù, yīnwèi méiyǒu shíjiān ('I didn't go, because I had no time') puts the result before yīnwèi -- but when the result comes second like that, suǒyǐ is dropped, since pairing yīnwèi...suǒyǐ that way would sound like the sentence is repeating itself.

dialogue.en: Why didn't you come?

dialogue.native: Yīnwèi wǒ bìng le, suǒyǐ méi lái.
dialogue.en: Because I was sick, so I didn't come.
Are you feeling a bit better now?

pairs.native: Nǐ néng gěi wǒ fā ge yóujiàn ma?
pairs.en: Can you send me an email?

lessons.title: A Trip to Beijing
lessons.description: A short recount of a family trip to Beijing last summer.

readingPassage.context: A short recount of a family trip to Beijing last summer.

paragraphs.native: Qùnián xiàtiān, wǒ hé jiārén qù le Běijīng lǚyóu.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 去年夏天，我和家人去了北京旅游。
paragraphs.en: Last summer, I went to Beijing with my family for a trip.

paragraphs.native: Wǒmen zuò fēijī qù, fēi le sān gè xiǎoshí.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 我们坐飞机去，飞了三个小时。
paragraphs.en: We went by plane, and the flight took three hours.

paragraphs.native: Dì yī tiān, wǒmen qù le Chángchéng. Nàlǐ rén hěn duō, dànshì fēngjǐng fēicháng měi.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 第一天，我们去了长城。那里人很多，但是风景非常美。
paragraphs.en: On the first day, we visited the Great Wall. There were many people there, but the scenery was extremely beautiful.

paragraphs.native: Dì èr tiān, tiānqì bú tài hǎo, xià le yìdiǎn yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒmen qù le bówùguǎn.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 第二天，天气不太好，下了一点雨，所以我们去了博物馆。
paragraphs.en: On the second day, the weather wasn't great, it rained a little, so we went to a museum.

paragraphs.native: Wǒmen hái chī le hěn duō hǎochī de Běijīng cài, bǐrú kǎoyā.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 我们还吃了很多好吃的北京菜，比如烤鸭。
paragraphs.en: We also ate a lot of delicious Beijing food, such as roast duck.

paragraphs.native: Zuìhòu yì tiān, wǒmen mǎi le hěn duō lǐwù, ránhòu zuò fēijī huí jiā.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 最后一天，我们买了很多礼物，然后坐飞机回家。
paragraphs.en: On the last day, we bought a lot of gifts, then flew home.

paragraphs.native: Zhè cì lǚxíng hěn yǒuyìsi, wǒ hěn xǐhuan Běijīng.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 这次旅行很有意思，我很喜欢北京。
paragraphs.en: This trip was very interesting, I really liked Beijing.

lessons.title: Weekend Plans
lessons.description: Xiao Li calls her friend Dawei to make plans for the weekend.

readingPassage.context: Xiao Li calls her friend Dawei to make plans for the weekend.

paragraphs.native: Xīngqíwǔ xiàwǔ, Xiǎo Lì gěi tā de péngyou Dàwěi dǎ diànhuà.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 星期五下午，小丽给她的朋友大伟打电话。
paragraphs.en: On Friday afternoon, Xiao Li called her friend Dawei.

paragraphs.native: Tā wèn Dàwěi zhōumò yǒu méiyǒu kòng.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 她问大伟周末有没有空。
paragraphs.en: She asked Dawei if he was free on the weekend.

paragraphs.native: Dàwěi shuō xīngqīliù shàngwǔ yào gōngzuò, dànshì xiàwǔ yǒu kòng.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 大伟说星期六上午要工作，但是下午有空。
paragraphs.en: Dawei said he had to work Saturday morning, but was free in the afternoon.

paragraphs.native: Xiǎo Lì jiànyì tāmen qù kàn diànyǐng, ránhòu yìqǐ chīfàn.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 小丽建议他们去看电影，然后一起吃饭。
paragraphs.en: Xiao Li suggested they go see a movie, then eat together.

paragraphs.native: Dàwěi juéde zhège zhǔyi hěn hǎo, tā hěn gāoxìng.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 大伟觉得这个主意很好，他很高兴。
paragraphs.en: Dawei thought it was a great idea, he was happy.

paragraphs.native: Tāmen yuē hǎo xiàwǔ sì diǎn zài diànyǐngyuàn ménkǒu jiàn miàn.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 他们约好下午四点在电影院门口见面。
paragraphs.en: They agreed to meet at the cinema entrance at 4pm.

paragraphs.native: Xīngqīliù dào le, tiānqì hěn hǎo, tāmen dùguò le yí gè yúkuài de xiàwǔ.
paragraphs.nativeHanzi: 星期六到了，天气很好，他们度过了一个愉快的下午。
paragraphs.en: Saturday came, the weather was nice, and they spent a pleasant afternoon.

exercises.question: What did they plan to do?
options: See a movie and eat together
